intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1F (CMT1F) is caused by heterozygous or homozygous mutation in the NEFL gene (162280) on chromosome 8p21.2.

checks.evidence_quote: We detected four heterozygous missense mutations--Pro8Leu, Glu90Lys, Asn98Ser and Glu396Lys--in five unrelated patients and a homozygous nonsense mutation, Glu140Stop, in one other patient.

checks.evidence_quote: The neurofilament light chain polypeptide (NEFL) forms the major intermediate filament in neurons and axons.

paragraphs.text: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1F (CMT1F) is a peripheral neuropathy caused by mutation in the NEFL gene. Jordanova et al. (2003) found that patients with NEFL mutations had early onset, often with a severe clinical phenotype, and moderately to severely slowed nerve conduction velocities. Both dominant and recessive forms have been reported. Abe et al. (2009) suggested that heterozygous missense mutations cause a dominant phenotype and nonsense mutations probably cause a recessive one.

checks.claim: CMT1F is a peripheral neuropathy caused by mutation in the NEFL gene.
checks.evidence_quote: NEFL mutation is a cause of axonal or demyelinating forms of dominant Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT).
checks.explanation: The abstract says NEFL mutation causes CMT, a peripheral neuropathy, but it doesn't use the CMT1F designation.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) described a 2-generation Palestinian family with first-cousin parents in which 4 of 5 children had a severe, progressive neuropathy starting at about 1.5 years of age. All 4 had hypotonia in infancy and early childhood, mildly delayed motor milestones, slowly progressive distal atrophy and weakness of the feet and hands, and bilateral pes cavus. All had moderate glove-and-stocking sensory impairment and absent ankle jerks, with CMT neuropathy scores of 16 to 27. One patient used a walker; the others walked with molded ankle-foot orthoses. None had pathologic reflexes, enlarged nerves, foot ulcers, cranial neuropathies, or clinically evident hearing loss. One patient had learning difficulties, and brain MRI was normal in the 3 patients scanned. On nerve conduction studies, sensory responses were absent in nearly all nerves tested. Median and ulnar motor conduction velocities were severely slowed (12 to 25 m/s) from early childhood, and amplitudes fell progressively with age. Peroneal and tibial responses eventually became unobtainable, and EMG showed severe distal denervation. Visual evoked responses were prolonged in 3 of the 4 affected children, which the authors took to indicate subclinical involvement of central nervous system axons.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) examined a sural nerve biopsy from 1 affected member of the Palestinian family at age 16 years. Myelinated axon density was reduced to 1,300/mm, compared with about 6,000/mm in controls. All myelinated axons were less than 3 microns in diameter, many were irregular in shape, and they lacked intermediate filaments while still containing microtubules. There were occasional clusters of regenerated axons but no actively degenerating axons. Axons stained with an N-terminal NFL antiserum but not with a C-terminal one, and they were immunoreactive for NFM, NFH, peripherin, and alpha-internexin. The authors concluded that the patients have indolent but progressive axonal loss.

paragraphs.text: In the 4 affected children of a consanguineous Palestinian family with severe early-onset neuropathy, Yum et al. (2009) sequenced NEFL and found a homozygous c.628G-T transversion predicted to cause a nonsense change at codon 210 (E210X). Both parents were heterozygous, and the unaffected sib did not carry the mutation. No mutations were found in PMP22, GJB1, MPZ, EGR2, PRX, LMNA, GDAP1, or MFN2, and there was no PMP22 duplication or deletion. The mutation was not found in more than 11,000 individuals tested at Athena Diagnostics. In SW-13 vim- cells, the mutant did not form filaments and did not interfere with filament formation by wildtype NFL, consistent with loss of function. The authors described this as the first recessive NEFL mutation.

paragraphs.text: Yum et al. (2009) noted that the conduction velocities in their patients fell within the 'demyelinating' range. Because NEFL is not prominently expressed by myelinating Schwann cells, they concluded that the absence of large myelinated axons, which lack neurofilaments, was the likely explanation for the slowed conduction. They suggested that neurofilaments determine axonal caliber and conduction velocity and are needed to maintain myelinated peripheral nerve axons.

paragraphs.text: In 4 affected children of a consanguineous Palestinian family with severe early-onset neuropathy, Yum et al. (2009) identified a homozygous c.628G-T transversion in the NEFL gene, predicted to result in a glu210-to-ter (E210X) substitution. Both parents were heterozygous, and the unaffected sib did not carry the mutation. The mutation was not found in more than 11,000 individuals tested at Athena Diagnostics. A sural nerve biopsy from 1 patient showed axons that stained with an N-terminal NFL antiserum but not with a C-terminal one. In SW-13 vim- cells, the mutant did not form filaments, showed a diffuse, mostly nuclear pattern, produced a poorly accumulating truncated band of about 30 kD, and did not interfere with filament formation by wildtype NFL, leading the authors to conclude that E210X causes a simple loss of function.
